paragraphs: Private stochastic convex optimization must balance finding a good solution with protecting the data used to compute it. Bounds designed for arbitrary convex functions can overlook useful structure in a particular problem. This paper develops algorithms that adapt to how quickly the objective rises as one moves away from its optimum.

The relevant structure is a growth condition with exponent κ greater than one. For functions satisfying this condition, the authors improve the privacy rate from √d/(nε) to (√d/(nε)) raised to κ/(κ−1). Crucially, the algorithms obtain this adaptation without knowing κ beforehand. They combine an inverse sensitivity mechanism, which responds to instance difficulty, with localization techniques in private optimization.

Matching lower bounds show that the improvements reflect the achievable accuracy for these function classes. The authors also establish simultaneous minimax optimality across κ ≥ 1+c when c is a positive constant of constant order. Thus, the contribution is both better rates under a stated growth condition and adaptation across those conditions without advance knowledge of the exponent.
neurips-2021-adapting-to-function-diffic.tldr: Private optimization algorithms achieve faster, optimal privacy rates by adapting to an objective’s growth near its optimum without knowing its growth exponent.

paragraphs: Many optimization methods depend on global bounds on how quickly an objective or its gradient can change. Some convex problems fail these standard continuity or smoothness requirements, particularly when their objectives have singular behavior. This paper considers a broader setting in which regularity is measured relative to a reference Bregman function.

Changing the reference geometry allows the analysis to describe objectives that do not behave regularly under a fixed ambient norm. The class includes problems such as Fisher markets, Poisson tomography, and D-design. The authors identify a gap here: existing adaptive methods such as UnixGrad and AcceleGrad cannot be applied in this setting, especially with randomness or uncertainty.

Their proposed family of methods centers on adaptive mirror descent, called AdaMir. It is designed to obtain minimax-optimal rates across relatively continuous and relatively smooth problems, including stochastic ones. The intended advantage is a single adaptive approach that responds to these different forms of regularity. Its scope still rests on relative regularity with respect to a reference function, rather than dispensing with structural conditions altogether.
neurips-2021-adaptive-first-order-method.tldr: AdaMir targets optimal adaptive convex optimization rates when regularity holds relative to a Bregman function instead of a global norm.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with rich observations often relies on realizability: the model class must accurately represent the relevant optimal value function. This paper studies an agnostic alternative. The learner has a fixed policy class Π, but that class may contain no policy close to the environment’s overall optimum.

The authors give an algorithm whose guarantees depend on the rank d of the underlying Markov decision process. Its sample complexity is Õ(H^(4d) K^(3d) log|Π| / ε²), where H is episode length, K is the number of actions, and ε is the desired suboptimality. The policy class enters logarithmically through its size, while episode length and action count have exponents determined by rank.

A nearly matching lower bound shows that exponential dependence on rank cannot generally be removed in this agnostic setting without additional assumptions. This gives the upper bound an important interpretation: allowing an imperfect policy class has an intrinsic statistical cost. The work therefore supplies both a learning guarantee under weaker representational expectations and evidence explaining a central difficulty of that setting.
neurips-2021-agnostic-reinforcement-lear.tldr: An agnostic reinforcement learning algorithm handles imperfect policy classes, with nearly matching bounds showing unavoidable exponential dependence on MDP rank.

paragraphs: Design synthesis asks for a configuration that meets constraints while achieving a desired objective. Several different designs can produce the same outcome, making the inverse mapping from goals to designs difficult to learn through supervision. Physical simulators introduce another obstacle when they cannot provide derivatives for direct optimization.

The paper addresses both issues with a two-stage neural architecture. First, it trains a differentiable surrogate to predict the physical outcome of a design. It then fixes this surrogate and trains a second network to map goals to designs, evaluating those designs through the surrogate. This resembles an autoencoder whose decoder is learned first and then used to train its encoder.

The authors evaluate the approach on extruder path planning for additive manufacturing and constrained soft robot inverse kinematics. In these cases, it produces higher-quality solutions than supervised synthesis. Its solution quality is also competitive with directly optimizing designs through the learned surrogate, while requiring much less computation. The result supports amortizing synthesis into a trained goal-to-design mapping for these tasks.
neurips-2021-amortized-synthesis-of-cons.tldr: A learned physical surrogate trains a goal-to-design network that produces competitive constrained designs at much lower computational cost in two case studies.

paragraphs: A backdoored neural network can behave normally on ordinary inputs but change its behavior when a trigger is present. Making that trigger visually imperceptible does not necessarily conceal the attack inside the model. Existing defenses can exploit differences between the internal representations of clean and triggered inputs.

This paper introduces Wasserstein Backdoor, which aims to hide those differences as well as the visible trigger. Its objective combines imperceptible input modifications with a Wasserstein-based regularizer that aligns the empirical distributions of clean and modified representations. The authors formulate this as a constrained, nonconvex optimization problem and solve it using stochastic alternating optimization.

Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR10, GTSRB, and TinyImagenet report high attack success alongside stealth in both input and representation spaces. The approach improves effectiveness against existing defenses, especially those depending on distinguishable internal features. The finding is that visual concealment and representational concealment can be pursued together, challenging defenses whose evidence comes from a separation between clean and backdoor feature distributions.
neurips-2021-backdoor-attack-with-imperc.tldr: Wasserstein Backdoor conceals triggers in both inputs and internal representations, improving attack effectiveness against tested defenses that rely on feature differences.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning shares a model across several objectives, often training it to minimize their average loss. The difficulty is that task gradients can point in conflicting directions. A step that improves the average can harm an individual task, undermining the benefits of sharing compared with training separate models.

Conflict-Averse Gradient descent, or CAGrad, retains average loss as its optimization objective while using the worst local improvement among tasks to regularize its trajectory. This makes individual task progress part of the update decision. The method automatically balances objectives and has a proof of convergence to a minimum of the average loss.

CAGrad also includes ordinary gradient descent and the multiple gradient descent algorithm as special cases, linking it to established approaches in multi-objective optimization. Experiments on multi-task supervised learning and reinforcement learning show improvements over prior state-of-the-art gradient manipulation methods. The contribution combines empirical gains with a specified optimization target, rather than providing only a heuristic for reconciling conflicting task directions.
neurips-2021-conflict-averse-gradient-de.tldr: CAGrad accounts for the worst local task improvement while minimizing average loss, with convergence guarantees and gains on tested multi-task problems.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed noise can make the variance of stochastic gradient descent iterates diverge, preventing the use of analyses that require finite second moments. This paper establishes convergence guarantees for a class of strongly convex objectives when the noise depends on the current state and may have infinite variance.

The analysis assumes that a p-th noise moment exists for some p between one and two, excluding two. It introduces a Hessian condition called p-positive definiteness or semidefiniteness. This condition interpolates between familiar positive semidefiniteness at p=2 and diagonal dominance with nonnegative diagonal entries at p=1. Under the condition, the authors bound convergence to the global optimum using an Lᵖ measure of distance.

They also prove that appropriately scaled Polyak–Ruppert averages converge in distribution to a multivariate α-stable random vector. Together, these results show that infinite variance need not prevent ordinary SGD from converging, without modifying the loss or algorithm, within the analyzed class. The paper demonstrates implications for misspecified models trained with heavy-tailed data.
neurips-2021-convergence-rates-of-stocha.tldr: Under stated moment and Hessian conditions, ordinary SGD converges on strongly convex objectives even when its noise has infinite variance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately a discrete probability distribution can be estimated when data are distributed among users with limited communication. Each of n users observes m samples but can broadcast only ℓ bits. The question is how additional local observations interact with the communication budget and the size of the distribution’s domain.

The authors characterize minimax estimation error up to logarithmic factors across most regimes of interest. For small m, the ℓ₁ error decreases by a factor of √m as each user receives more samples. This extends the commonly studied setting in which each user holds only one observation and describes the benefit of having more local data.

For large m, the relationship changes qualitatively. The error’s dependence on the communication budget shifts from 1/√(2^ℓ) to 1/√ℓ. Thus, the same increase in transmitted bits has a different effect depending on how many observations each user holds. This phase transition shows why communication and local sample availability must be analyzed jointly when assessing distributed estimation accuracy.
neurips-2021-distributed-estimation-with.tldr: Nearly tight estimation bounds reveal that communication has a different effect on accuracy when users hold many samples instead of few.

paragraphs: First-order, or small-loss, guarantees let learning performance improve when the best available hypothesis incurs little loss. Obtaining this kind of adaptation is challenging in contextual bandits, where decisions determine the feedback available to the learner. This paper resolves an open question about whether efficient algorithms can achieve such guarantees.

The authors give an optimal, efficient reduction from contextual bandits to online regression using logarithmic, or cross-entropy, loss. It accommodates rich function classes and requires no distributional assumption beyond realizability. The reduction makes the prediction problem’s loss choice central to obtaining a decision-making guarantee that adapts to easier instances.

The analysis connects logarithmic loss with triangular discrimination, an information-theoretic measure, and refines the regression-oracle reduction framework. This connection also produces new results for classical statistical learning. In a large empirical evaluation, the proposed approach typically outperforms comparable methods without first-order guarantees. The theoretical and experimental findings therefore support small-loss adaptation, with the empirical advantage stated as typical rather than universal.
neurips-2021-efficient-first-order-conte.tldr: An efficient reduction to logarithmic-loss regression gives contextual bandits optimal small-loss guarantees under realizability.

paragraphs: Different organizations or local systems may each hold only a small collection of graphs, creating a reason to train graph neural networks collaboratively. The authors find statistically significant shared properties across real-world graph domains. However, graph collections also differ in structure and node features, even within one domain or dataset.

Graph Clustered Federated Learning, or GCFL, addresses this heterogeneity by dynamically grouping local systems using their GNN gradients. The paper provides theoretical justification that these clusters can reduce differences in graph structure and features within the groups. The approach uses training signals to determine which systems should collaborate more closely.

The authors also observe that individual gradients fluctuate enough to interfere with clustering. Their extension, GCFL+, compares sequences of gradients using dynamic time warping, making the grouping mechanism sensitive to gradient histories. Experiments and further analysis support the effectiveness of both frameworks. The overall contribution is a way to organize federated graph learning around differences between local datasets while still exploiting their potential shared structure.
neurips-2021-federated-graph-classificat.tldr: GCFL and GCFL+ cluster federated graph learners using gradients and gradient histories to address differences in graph structures and node features.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning must learn from training signals that can contain substantial optimization noise. This paper proposes embedding inputs into a learned Fourier basis before processing them with a network. The architecture improves sample efficiency in experiments involving both state observations and image observations.

An infinite-width analysis using the Neural Tangent Kernel explains how the initialization of these features affects learning. The authors show that changing the Fourier basis’s initial variance corresponds to functional regularization of the network. In particular, it controls the degree to which different frequencies in the data are underfit or overfit, providing a way to influence which patterns the network learns.

Empirically, the method prioritizes low-frequency functions and speeds learning by reducing susceptibility to noise, including noise arising during Bellman updates. Standard state-based and image-based reinforcement learning benchmarks show clear benefits over the evaluated baselines. The contribution connects a simple architectural choice to a theoretical account of frequency-dependent regularization, then demonstrates its usefulness for reinforcement learning optimization.
neurips-2021-functional-regularization-f.tldr: Learned Fourier features regulate which frequencies a reinforcement learning network fits and improve sample efficiency on state-based and image-based benchmarks.

paragraphs: Training beyond zero training error can make conventional remedies for class imbalance, such as weighted cross-entropy, ineffective. This paper analyzes how changes to classification losses influence margins in that terminal phase. It addresses both unequal label frequencies and group-sensitive objectives such as equal opportunity.

For linear classifiers trained in the terminal phase, the authors prove that multiplicative logit adjustments are necessary to change interclass margins appropriately. They connect this result to cost-sensitive support-vector machines. Yet the same multiplicative weights can hurt minority classes early in training. Additive adjustments, though ineffective for the terminal-phase margin change, can counter this early harm and accelerate convergence.

These complementary roles motivate vector-scaling loss, which includes existing techniques as special cases and extends to group-sensitive classification. Experiments agree with the theoretical insights and show superior performance for the proposed algorithms. A separate generalization analysis for imbalanced Gaussian mixtures exposes tradeoffs among balanced error, standard error, and equal opportunity, clarifying that the choice of performance objective matters.
neurips-2021-label-imbalanced-and-group-.tldr: An analysis of early and late training motivates vector-scaling loss for label imbalance and group-sensitive classification.

paragraphs: This paper studies limits on two widely used sampling methods: the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm, or MALA, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, or HMC, with leapfrog integration. Its focus is well-conditioned target distributions. Lower bounds identify settings where these algorithms must take substantial time, even though the targets have favorable conditioning.

For MALA, the main result is a mixing-time lower bound of approximately κd, ignoring logarithmic factors, from an exponentially warm start. Here κ represents conditioning and d is dimension. The bound matches existing algorithmic results up to logarithmic factors, establishing that their dependence on these quantities is nearly tight in the stated setting.

For HMC, the authors prove that relaxation time must have polynomial dependence on dimension regardless of the number of leapfrog steps. They also bound how much changing that step count can help. The analysis develops a connection between leapfrog integration and Chebyshev polynomials. Together, the findings clarify limits on convergence speed and on improvements obtainable through this HMC tuning choice.
neurips-2021-lower-bounds-on-metropolize.tldr: Nearly tight MALA bounds and dimension-dependent HMC bounds establish limits on sampling speed even for well-conditioned distributions.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can generalize poorly when only a small portion of their data is labeled. Data augmentation offers a possible remedy, but graph structure and dependencies between samples complicate the design of useful transformations. This paper proposes an approach that specifies a target distribution over augmented graphs.

The framework, Metropolis-Hastings Data Augmentation or MH-Aug, generates a sequence of graphs according to that distribution. An explicit target gives control over both the strength and diversity of augmentation. Because directly sampling from the target can be difficult, the method uses the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm to obtain the augmented samples.

The authors also introduce a semi-supervised learning strategy that uses the generated graphs. Experiments show that MH-Aug can produce samples following the target distribution and significantly improve GNN performance. The contribution connects augmentation design to a sampling problem: the desired variation is expressed through a distribution, and a sampling method supplies graphs for training. This provides a structured way to control augmentation in the sparsely labeled setting studied.
neurips-2021-metropolis-hastings-data-au.tldr: MH-Aug samples augmented graphs from an explicit target distribution to control augmentation and improve semi-supervised GNN performance.

paragraphs: Generating a whole method requires maintaining relationships across a longer stretch of code than generating an expression or a single line. Neural code models often struggle with these longer tasks. This paper introduces weak supervision from a static program analyzer to help a generative model account for such relationships.

The method combines neural generation with symbolic analysis. Calls to the analyzer compute long-distance semantic relationships in code the model has already produced. During training, the model observes these relationships and learns to condition further generation on them. The approach therefore gives the generator explicit information about its developing program.

The authors evaluate generation of complete Java methods given the rest of the containing class. Their method substantially outperforms a state-of-the-art transformer and a model that explicitly learns program semantics, both in avoiding basic semantic errors and in syntactically matching the reference code. These results support static analysis as useful supervision for longer code-generation tasks, while the reported evaluation concerns those specific measures rather than complete program correctness.
neurips-2021-neural-program-generation-m.tldr: Conditioning neural code generation on static-analysis relationships improves whole-method Java generation on semantic-error and syntactic-match measures.

paragraphs: Comparing neural networks for tabular data is difficult when papers use different datasets, training procedures, and tuning protocols. This paper reviews major architecture families and evaluates models under shared conditions. Its goal is to identify useful baselines and make performance comparisons easier to interpret.

The study highlights two relatively simple architectures. A ResNet-like model provides a strong baseline that earlier work often omitted. The authors also introduce a straightforward adaptation of the Transformer for tabular inputs, which outperforms other solutions on most evaluated tasks. Both models are compared with many existing architectures across a diverse collection of tasks using the same training and tuning protocols.

The paper further compares the strongest deep learning models with gradient boosted decision trees. That comparison finds no universally superior solution. The practical message is therefore twofold: tabular deep learning benefits from stronger, accessible reference models, and model choice still depends on the problem. The Transformer’s success across most tasks does not establish that neural networks dominate every tabular setting.
neurips-2021-revisiting-deep-learning-mo.tldr: Consistent comparisons identify strong ResNet-like and Transformer baselines for tabular data, while finding no universal winner over boosted trees.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new policy would perform using data collected by another policy. Trajectory importance sampling can provide unbiased estimates, but its variance can be high. Methods based on state-action visitation distributions often reduce variance over long horizons, yet estimating their distribution ratios can introduce bias.

SOPE places these two approaches at opposite ends of a spectrum of estimators. This gives a new way to understand and adjust their bias-variance tradeoff. The paper also establishes corresponding spectra for weighted estimators and doubly robust estimators, extending the perspective beyond the basic importance-sampling formulations.

The empirical results show that intermediate estimators can achieve lower mean-squared error than either endpoint. This means that accepting some of one method’s weaknesses in exchange for reducing the other’s can improve overall estimation accuracy. The finding supports considering a range of estimators when evaluating a policy from historical data. It does not assert that a particular intermediate choice always dominates both endpoints across all problems.
neurips-2021-sope-spectrum-of-off-policy.tldr: SOPE connects trajectory and visitation-distribution importance sampling through estimator families that can improve the bias-variance tradeoff.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent-ascent and stochastic consensus optimization are prominent methods for smooth games, including adversarial optimization problems. Their theoretical treatment has gaps: existing SGDA analyses require bounded variance, while convergence guarantees for consensus optimization have been limited to its deterministic version. This paper develops guarantees using expected co-coercivity.

Under this condition, the authors establish convergence of the last iterate for a class of stochastic variational inequality problems that can be non-monotone. With a constant step size, both algorithms converge linearly to a neighborhood of the solution. The guarantee therefore describes rapid approach to a region around the answer, rather than exact convergence under that step-size choice.

The paper then supplies step-size switching rules that guarantee convergence to the exact solution. Its analysis also permits arbitrary sampling, allowing the authors to examine the complexity of minibatching. The contribution is a shared theoretical framework for the two stochastic methods, with explicit distinctions between constant-step behavior and the stronger convergence obtained by changing the step size.
neurips-2021-stochastic-gradient-descent.tldr: Expected co-coercivity yields last-iterate guarantees for stochastic descent-ascent and consensus optimization, including exact convergence with step-size switching.

paragraphs: Iterative voting lets voters repeatedly change their ballots strategically until an equilibrium is reached. A winner’s initial vote count does not by itself describe how much voters value that outcome. This paper studies social welfare in iterative plurality while distinguishing voters’ utilities from the mechanism governing their strategic changes.

The authors analyze the additive dynamic price of anarchy, which compares welfare under truthful voting with welfare at the worst equilibrium reached through repeated manipulation. In the worst case, this welfare gap grows linearly with the number of voters. Strategic behavior can therefore have substantial negative consequences in unfavorable cases.

The average-case analysis gives a different result: equilibrium winners have a constant-order welfare advantage over the truthful winner in expectation. This establishes a positive possibility for strategic manipulation despite the worst-case bound. The distinction between the two analyses is essential. The paper shows that strategic behavior can improve expected welfare in the analyzed average-case setting, while retaining the possibility of large losses in particular cases.
neurips-2021-strategic-behavior-is-bliss.tldr: Iterative plurality can improve welfare in expectation under the paper’s average-case analysis, despite welfare losses that scale linearly in the worst case.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning often depends on augmentations that exploit structure in images, audio, or text. Tables may lack comparable spatial, temporal, or semantic organization, making suitable augmentations harder to design. SubTab approaches this problem by treating different subsets of a table’s features as multiple views of the same example.

The framework trains representations through reconstruction from feature subsets. The authors argue that this can capture underlying latent structure better than reconstructing from a corrupted input in an autoencoder. At test time, the representations of the different subsets are aggregated into a joint representation, a process they call collaborative inference.

Experiments report 98.31% performance on MNIST treated as tabular data, described as state of the art and comparable to CNN-based state-of-the-art models. SubTab also surpasses the evaluated baselines by a significant margin on three other real-world datasets. These findings support feature subsetting as a useful route to self-supervised tabular representations, with the reported gains tied to the datasets and comparisons in the study.
neurips-2021-subtab-subsetting-features-.tldr: SubTab learns tabular representations from feature subsets and combines their latent representations, achieving strong results on four evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Recovering a sparse vector’s support means identifying which of its coordinates are nonzero. This paper considers several unknown sparse vectors whose measurements are randomly mixed together. The learner must identify each vector’s support without knowing which component produced a given observation.

The authors study mixtures of linear regressions and mixtures of linear classifiers. Regression measurements reveal a projection of a randomly selected unknown vector, while classifier measurements reveal which side of a queried hyperplane it lies on. The latter provides only a one-bit observation. The framework considers small numbers of measurements that may also be noisy.

The paper gives algorithms that recover all component supports with high probability. For ℓ vectors, each with at most k nonzero coordinates in n dimensions, the sufficient measurement count is polynomial in k and log n and quasi-polynomial in ℓ. These guarantees identify a way to exploit sparsity despite mixing. They concern support identification, described as a primary step toward recovering the unknown vectors, rather than full recovery of every coordinate value.
neurips-2021-support-recovery-of-sparse-.tldr: Algorithms recover every sparse component’s support from mixed linear or one-bit measurements with high-probability measurement guarantees.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning often requires agents to evaluate a policy without centralizing the computation. This paper studies that problem with nonlinear function approximation. Both the amount of data processed and the communication between agents matter for making such evaluation efficient.

The authors reformulate empirical decentralized policy evaluation as a minimax saddle-point problem that is nonconvex in one variable and strongly concave in the other. They introduce a gradient descent-ascent algorithm, GT-GDA, followed by two stochastic variants, GT-SRVR and GT-SRVRI. The latter use variance reduction to reduce sample requirements.

All three methods have an O(1/T) convergence rate to a stationary point of the reformulated problem. The variance-reduced methods achieve O(ε⁻²) communication complexity and O(m√n ε⁻²) sample complexity, where m counts agents and n is trajectory length. Thus, both costs have the same ε⁻² accuracy dependence, while sample cost also depends on agents and trajectory length. Experiments corroborate the theoretical performance. The convergence target remains a stationary point of the stated nonconvex formulation.
neurips-2021-taming-communication-and-sa.tldr: Variance-reduced decentralized algorithms evaluate cooperative policies with ε⁻² dependence in both communication and sample complexity.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds describe the expected gap between a model’s performance on its training data and on new data. This paper develops bounds using Wasserstein distance, which can incorporate the geometry of the hypothesis space. It provides full-dataset, single-letter, and random-subset versions, together with counterparts for a randomized subsample setting.

The authors connect these bounds to existing approaches based on relative entropy. When the loss is bounded and the chosen Wasserstein metric ignores geometry, the new bounds recover those earlier bounds from below, making them tighter in that setting. The results also yield new relative-entropy bounds that are non-vacuous, meaning they provide informative control.

This establishes a bridge between geometric analyses and information-theoretic analyses that do not use geometry. The paper further derives bounds involving other information measures, including lautum information and several f-divergences. Its proof techniques also produce analogous bounds for the backward channel. The contribution is therefore a family of related guarantees, with the tighter comparison to relative entropy tied to the stated bounded-loss and metric conditions.
neurips-2021-tighter-expected-generaliza.tldr: Wasserstein-based generalization bounds connect geometric and information-theoretic analyses and tighten relative-entropy bounds under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Image restoration must recover both the broad content of an image and its fine spatial details. This paper argues that conventional end-to-end networks do not sufficiently reflect this structure of the task. It uses Taylor approximations as a guide for building a restoration framework with distinct roles for context and detail.

The proposed architecture unfolds Taylor’s formula into two corresponding functions. A mapping function first learns high-level contextual information. A derivative function then combines that information with the degraded input to progressively recover local, higher-order spatial detail. The authors relate these roles to the main and derivative parts of a Taylor approximation.

This organization supplies a rationale for how the restoration process is divided, connecting the network design to the two competing demands of the task. The framework can be integrated with existing methods, allowing it to complement their architectures. Extensive experiments support its effectiveness and scalability. The reported contribution is thus both a Taylor-inspired decomposition of restoration and evidence that this decomposition can improve existing approaches.
neurips-2021-unfolding-taylor-s-approxim.tldr: A Taylor-inspired restoration framework learns global context first and progressively reconstructs local detail, with experimental support for integration into existing methods.

paragraphs: Width reduction has improved iteration counts for optimization problems such as maximum flow and ℓₚ regression, from O(m¹ᐟ²) to roughly O(m¹ᐟ³), with each iteration requiring a linear-system solve. Here m is the number of design-matrix rows. A drawback is that earlier methods needed potentials and analyses tailored to each problem.

This paper develops a unified width-reduction approach for a broader class of constrained convex optimization problems. Its central extension covers quasi-self-concordant losses, including logistic regression. The algorithms also address problems such as softmax and ℓₚ regression. A more general family of potentials provides the basis for handling these objectives within a shared framework.

The method achieves m¹ᐟ³-type iteration rates directly in the constrained setting without explicit acceleration schemes. This matters because the improvement is attached to a reusable analytical approach rather than a separate construction for each objective. The result broadens the reach of width reduction while retaining the improved dependence on the number of rows, complementing approaches based on ball oracles.
neurips-2021-unifying-width-reduced-meth.tldr: A unified width-reduction framework achieves m¹ᐟ³-type iteration rates for constrained convex problems including quasi-self-concordant losses.
